To find the last digit in base 6, we need the remainder when 355 is divided by 6.

\(355 \div 6 = 59\) remainder \(1\), since \(6 \cdot 59 = 354\).

So the base 6 representation of 355 ends in **1**.

the social network is one of the sharpest and most compelling films of the 21st century, a movie that turns the creation of facebook into a tense, emotionally charged story about ambition, loneliness, betrayal, and the cost of genius. directed by david fincher and written by aaron sorkin, it is not just a film about a website being built; it is a film about the kind of people who build empires and the damage they leave behind.

what makes the movie so effective is how it transforms a relatively recent and familiar piece of history into something that feels almost like a tragedy. mark zuckerberg, played with icy precision by jesse eisenberg, is not presented as a simple villain or hero. he is brilliant, insecure, socially awkward, and deeply driven by the need to be recognized. eisenberg’s performance captures the character’s speed of thought and emotional distance, making him fascinating even when he is difficult to like. he speaks in rapid, cutting bursts, and every line feels like it is trying to prove something. at the same time, the film suggests that his intelligence is inseparable from his inability to connect with people in a healthy way.

the screenplay is one of the film’s greatest strengths. sorkin’s dialogue is fast, witty, and loaded with subtext. conversations often feel like verbal duels, where every sentence is a move in a larger power struggle. the script never wastes time explaining things in a dull or mechanical way. instead, it lets the conflict emerge through argument, accusation, and humiliation. even scenes that are mostly people talking in rooms feel suspenseful because the stakes are always clear: status, ownership, loyalty, and control.

fincher’s direction gives the film a cold, controlled atmosphere that perfectly matches its subject. the visual style is sleek and restrained, with dark interiors, muted colors, and a constant sense of pressure. the movie moves with precision, never feeling rushed even though the dialogue is often extremely fast. fincher understands that the story is not really about coding or business strategy, but about human relationships breaking under the weight of ego and resentment. his direction keeps the film emotionally distant in a way that mirrors mark’s own detachment, which makes the moments of vulnerability hit even harder.

the supporting cast is excellent across the board. andrew garfield brings real emotional depth to eduardo saverin, the co-founder whose loyalty is gradually betrayed. garfield makes eduardo sympathetic without turning him into a saint; you can feel his hurt, confusion, and anger as the friendship collapses. justin timberlake is also memorable as sean parker, the charismatic and manipulative napster founder who helps pull facebook into a more aggressive, more glamorous future. timberlake plays him with a mix of charm and menace that makes him feel like a dangerous influence rather than a simple opportunist. armie hammer’s dual performance as the winklevoss twins is both technically impressive and thematically fitting, since the film is full of doubles, mirrors, and competing versions of the truth.

one of the film’s most interesting achievements is that it makes legal and business disputes feel emotionally meaningful. the lawsuits are not just background noise; they are the structure through which the story is told. by moving back and forth between depositions and flashbacks, the film creates a sense that every success is already haunted by regret and accusation. this structure also reinforces the idea that history is messy and subjective. everyone believes they were wronged, everyone has a version of events, and the truth is filtered through pride and memory.

the film’s emotional core is arguably not facebook itself, but mark’s inability to maintain genuine human connection. the opening scene between mark and erica, played by rooney mara, is crucial because it establishes the central wound of the movie. mark’s need to impress, dominate, and outthink others destroys the relationship before it can really begin. from that point on, the film keeps returning to the idea that his success may be a substitute for intimacy. he can build a platform that connects millions of people, but he cannot seem to connect with the people closest to him.

the score by trent reznor and atticus ross deserves special praise. it is eerie, propulsive, and emotionally unsettling, giving the film a modern, almost mechanical pulse. the music helps create the feeling that the story is unfolding inside a machine that is constantly accelerating. it is one of those scores that becomes inseparable from the movie itself, enhancing the tension without ever overwhelming it.

if the film has a weakness, it is that some viewers may find its emotional perspective somewhat narrow. because the story is so focused on mark, the other characters can sometimes feel like they exist mainly to reflect his flaws or ambitions. that said, this limitation also seems intentional. the movie is about a man whose worldview is so self-centered that everyone else becomes part of his orbit. whether that makes him more understandable or more alienating depends on the viewer, but it is certainly consistent.

overall, the social network is a brilliant, incisive, and highly rewatchable film. it works as a drama, a character study, a business story, and a cautionary tale about the social cost of obsession. it captures a specific moment in tech history while also feeling timeless in its exploration of envy, ambition, and isolation. it is stylish without being empty, intelligent without being cold, and emotionally devastating in ways that sneak up on you. it is easily one of fincher’s best films and one of the defining movies of its era.

the social network is one of the sharpest and most compelling films of the 2010s, and it remains impressive because it is not really just a movie about facebook. it is a movie about ambition, resentment, status, loneliness, and the way genius can be tangled up with cruelty. david fincher directs it with a cold, precise confidence that fits the story perfectly, and aaron sorkin’s screenplay gives the film a relentless pulse. every scene feels like it is moving at high speed, even when the characters are sitting still and talking.

jesse eisenberg is excellent as mark zuckerberg. he plays him not as a simple villain or a misunderstood hero, but as someone brilliant, insecure, defensive, and emotionally stunted. his performance is full of tiny shifts in tone that make mark feel both intimidating and pathetic. you can see how badly he wants recognition, even as he pretends not to care what anyone thinks. that contradiction is what makes the character so interesting. andrew garfield is equally strong as eduardo saverin, bringing warmth and hurt to a role that could have been one-dimensional. his betrayal carries real emotional weight because garfield makes eduardo feel like a genuine friend, not just a plot device. armie hammer’s dual performance as the winklevoss twins is also memorable, not only because of the technical trickery, but because he gives them a polished, entitled arrogance that suits the film’s themes of privilege and ownership.

one of the film’s greatest strengths is its structure. by framing the story through depositions and legal disputes, it turns the rise of facebook into a kind of modern myth told through conflict and accusation. this approach gives the movie momentum while also creating a sense of inevitability. we already know that success has come at a cost, so the tension comes from watching relationships break apart and watching people justify themselves in real time. the dialogue is fast, witty, and often brutal. sorkin writes conversations like verbal duels, and fincher stages them with a cool detachment that makes the words hit even harder.

the film also benefits from its visual style. fincher’s direction is controlled and elegant, using dark interiors, muted colors, and precise framing to create a world that feels emotionally isolated. even when the characters are surrounded by people, they often seem alone. the score by trent reznor and atticus ross is a huge part of that atmosphere. it is eerie, propulsive, and modern, giving the film a restless energy that mirrors the speed of the digital age. the music does not simply support the scenes; it deepens the feeling that something important and unsettling is happening beneath the surface.

what makes the social network especially effective is that it understands how personal and impersonal success can be at the same time. the film shows the creation of a world-changing platform, but it never loses sight of the petty emotions driving it: jealousy, exclusion, humiliation, and the desire to belong. mark’s genius is undeniable, but the movie is clear that intelligence alone does not make someone admirable. in fact, the film is most interesting when it asks whether mark’s success is a triumph or a kind of emotional failure. by the end, he has built something enormous, but he has also destroyed trust, friendship, and any real sense of connection.

if there is a criticism to make, it is that the film’s coolness can sometimes create distance. because it is so polished and so verbally agile, it can feel emotionally restrained in moments where a more vulnerable approach might have hit harder. but that restraint is also part of the film’s design, and it suits the subject. this is a story about people who are always performing intelligence and control, even when they are falling apart.

overall, the social network is a brilliant, tightly constructed drama that captures a specific moment in tech history while also feeling timeless. it is smart without being smug, stylish without being empty, and emotionally complex without becoming sentimental. it is a film about the cost of building something that changes the world, and about the loneliness that can remain when the work is done. even years later, it feels urgent, modern, and unsettlingly relevant.

the social network is one of the sharpest and most compelling films of the 21st century, and it remains just as impressive years after its release. directed by david fincher and written by aaron sorkin, the film turns the origin story of facebook into something far more interesting than a simple tech biography. instead of treating mark zuckerberg’s rise as a straightforward success story, it presents a tense, bitter, and emotionally layered drama about ambition, betrayal, loneliness, and the cost of genius.

one of the film’s greatest strengths is its screenplay. sorkin’s dialogue is fast, precise, and constantly engaging. every conversation feels like a duel, with characters trying to outthink, outmaneuver, or outtalk one another. the script is full of memorable lines, but it never feels like it is showing off for its own sake. beneath the wit and speed, there is real emotional weight. the film understands that the creation of facebook was not just a business event, but a moment that reshaped modern social life, and it uses that backdrop to explore deeply personal conflicts.

jesse eisenberg gives an outstanding performance as mark zuckerberg. he plays mark as brilliant, awkward, defensive, and emotionally distant, but never as a simple villain. eisenberg captures the character’s restless intelligence and social insecurity in a way that makes him fascinating even when he is difficult to like. his performance is subtle in some moments and explosive in others, and it anchors the entire film. alongside him, andrew garfield is excellent as eduardo saverin, bringing warmth and hurt to a character who becomes one of the film’s most tragic figures. justin timberlake also delivers a memorable turn as sean parker, giving the character a dangerous charm that makes him both magnetic and unsettling.

fincher’s direction is controlled and elegant. he gives the film a cold, polished visual style that fits its themes perfectly. the dark interiors, muted colors, and precise framing create a sense of emotional distance, as if the characters are always separated from one another even when they are in the same room. the pacing is excellent, and the film moves with a confidence that makes its complex structure feel effortless. the use of the dual timeline, shifting between depositions and flashbacks, adds tension and gives the story a sense of inevitability. we already know that relationships have broken apart, but the film keeps us invested in how and why that happened.

the score by trent reznor and atticus ross is another major achievement. it is eerie, propulsive, and strangely beautiful, helping to define the film’s mood. the music gives the story a modern, almost mechanical pulse, but it also carries sadness and unease. it is one of those scores that becomes inseparable from the film itself.

what makes the social network especially effective is that it refuses to be simplistic. it does not present mark as a pure genius or a pure monster. it does not reduce the story to a morality tale about greed, nor does it celebrate innovation without question. instead, it shows how ambition can distort relationships and how success can be built on resentment, insecurity, and the desire to be recognized. the film is about friendship, but it is also about exclusion. it is about wanting to belong while simultaneously pushing people away.

if there is any weakness, it is that some viewers may find the characters emotionally cold or difficult to connect with on a personal level. that distance is clearly intentional, but it can make the film feel more intellectually gripping than emotionally warm. even so, that coldness is part of what makes it so effective. the movie is not trying to comfort the audience; it is trying to expose the machinery of power and ego.

overall, the social network is a brilliant film: smart, stylish, tense, and deeply memorable. it combines exceptional writing, directing, acting, and music into a work that feels both specific to its time and timeless in its themes. it is not just a movie about facebook. it is a movie about ambition, alienation, and the price of creating something that changes the world. it deserves its reputation as a modern classic.

We have seasons because Earth is tilted as it goes around the Sun.

Imagine Earth like a spinning top that is leaning a little bit. That lean is called a tilt. As Earth travels around the Sun during the year, different parts of Earth get more sunlight or less sunlight.

- When your part of Earth is tilted toward the Sun, it gets more direct sunlight and longer days. That makes it warmer, so it’s summer.
- When your part of Earth is tilted away from the Sun, it gets less direct sunlight and shorter days. That makes it cooler, so it’s winter.
- Spring and fall happen in between, when the tilt is not giving one side a big advantage.

So seasons are not caused by how close Earth is to the Sun. They happen because Earth is tilted while it moves around the Sun.

P.S. A fun way to remember it: Earth’s tilt is like a flashlight shining on a tilted ball—different parts get more light at different times!

the social network is one of the sharpest and most compelling films of the 2010s, and it remains impressive because it is not really a movie about computers or even just about facebook. it is a movie about ambition, resentment, status, loneliness, and the way genius can be inseparable from cruelty. david fincher directs it with his usual precision, turning what could have been a straightforward biographical drama into something tense, elegant, and emotionally cold in exactly the right way.

the screenplay by aaron sorkin is the film’s greatest strength. the dialogue moves at a remarkable pace, full of wit, bite, and subtext. nearly every conversation feels like a duel, with characters trying to outthink, outmaneuver, or humiliate one another. sorkin makes legal disputes and business negotiations feel as dramatic as a thriller, and he does it without sacrificing clarity. even when the film jumps between timelines and perspectives, it remains easy to follow because the writing is so disciplined.

jesse eisenberg gives mark zuckerberg a brilliant, unsettling performance. he plays mark as brilliant, defensive, socially awkward, and deeply wounded, but never as a simple villain. what makes the performance so effective is that eisenberg captures both mark’s intelligence and his emotional immaturity. he seems constantly on the verge of saying something cutting, not because he is confident, but because he is afraid of being dismissed. that tension gives the character real depth. you can understand why people are drawn to him and why they are eventually repelled by him.

andrew garfield is equally strong as eduardo saverin. he brings warmth, loyalty, and a sense of genuine hurt to the role, which makes his betrayal feel especially painful. his performance gives the film its emotional center, because eduardo is one of the few characters who seems to want friendship more than power. armie hammer, playing both winklevoss twins with the help of digital effects, is surprisingly effective as well. he makes the twins feel polished, entitled, and absurdly self-serious, which fits the film’s tone perfectly. justin timberlake also stands out as sean parker, bringing charisma and danger to a role that could have been one-note. he plays parker as someone who understands the seduction of influence and knows exactly how to exploit it.

fincher’s direction is controlled and stylish without ever feeling showy. the film has a cold visual palette that suits its themes, and the pacing is relentless. even scenes of people sitting in rooms talking feel charged with momentum. the editing is especially strong, constantly moving between depositions, flashbacks, and moments of confrontation in a way that creates both suspense and irony. the score by trent reznor and atticus ross is another major asset. it is eerie, propulsive, and modern, giving the film a restless energy that matches the emotional unease underneath the story.

what makes the social network so memorable is that it refuses easy moralizing. it does not simply condemn mark zuckerberg, nor does it celebrate him. instead, it presents him as a product of a particular kind of culture: one obsessed with exclusivity, competition, and being first. the film suggests that facebook was born not just from technical brilliance, but from social insecurity and the desire to belong by controlling the terms of belonging for others. that idea gives the movie a lasting relevance, especially in an era when social media has become even more central to daily life.

Here’s a practical approach:

### 1. Play everywhere you can
Start with small venues, open mics, house shows, art spaces, cafes, and local festivals. The goal is to get your name circulating and build a reputation for showing up and delivering.

### 2. Make your live show memorable
People remember energy, not perfection. Have:
- a strong stage presence
- 1–2 signature moments in your set
- tight transitions
- a clear visual identity

If people leave saying “that band was insane live,” you’re on the right track.

### 3. Collaborate with local artists
Work with:
- other musicians
- DJs
- visual artists
- photographers
- promoters

Cross-pollination helps you tap into existing audiences instead of building everything from zero.

### 4. Be active in the scene, not just on stage
Go to other people’s shows. Support local acts. Talk to venue owners, sound engineers, promoters, and fans. Scenes are built on relationships.

### 5. Release music consistently
Even if it’s just singles or live sessions, keep putting out material. Pair releases with shows so people have something to follow after they discover you.

Post:
- clips from shows
- rehearsal snippets
- behind-the-scenes content
- announcements for local gigs
- short, shareable performance videos

- a unique sound
- a striking image
- a concept or theme
- a wild live setup
- a strong local identity

Don’t chase everyone. Get 20–50 people who genuinely care, show up, and bring friends. That’s often enough to create momentum.

Have:
- a simple EPK
- good photos
- a short bio
- links to music and videos
- contact info

“Exploding” usually looks like months of steady work that suddenly becomes visible. The scene notices people who keep showing up.

the social network is one of the sharpest and most compelling films of the 2010s, and it remains impressive because it is not really a movie about facebook so much as a movie about ambition, resentment, loneliness, and the way genius can be tangled up with cruelty. directed by david fincher and written by aaron sorkin, it turns a story about the creation of a website into something that feels almost shakespearean in its emotional stakes. the result is a film that is fast, intelligent, and surprisingly tragic.

one of the movie’s greatest strengths is its screenplay. sorkin’s dialogue moves with incredible speed, but it never feels empty or showy for its own sake. every conversation is loaded with subtext, especially in the scenes between mark zuckerberg and the people around him. mark is written as someone who is brilliant, defensive, insecure, and often deeply unpleasant, yet the film never reduces him to a simple villain. instead, it shows how his intelligence and his emotional immaturity feed each other. he wants recognition, but he cannot handle intimacy. he wants to be admired, but he also seems to resent the very people whose approval he craves.

jesse eisenberg gives a remarkable performance as mark zuckerberg. he plays him with a mix of nervous energy, arrogance, and wounded pride that makes the character fascinating even when he is behaving badly. eisenberg captures the speed of mark’s mind, but also the emptiness underneath it. there is a constant sense that mark is always trying to stay one step ahead of humiliation. that makes him compelling, but not exactly likable, and the film is smart enough to trust that distinction. it does not ask the audience to admire him; it asks the audience to understand him.

andrew garfield is equally strong as eduardo saverin, mark’s early friend and business partner. eduardo is one of the film’s most tragic figures because he believes in the friendship more sincerely than mark does. garfield brings warmth, frustration, and heartbreak to the role, and his scenes carry a real emotional sting. the betrayal at the center of the story lands because the film has taken the time to show how much eduardo invested in the relationship. his anger feels earned, not melodramatic.

armie hammer’s dual performance as the winklevoss twins is one of the film’s most memorable technical and acting achievements. the twins could have been a gimmick, but hammer makes them distinct while also emphasizing their shared entitlement and frustration. they are privileged, disciplined, and convinced that the world owes them something. their scenes add a layer of irony to the story, because they are both victims of mark’s ruthlessness and representatives of a social world that also runs on status and exclusion.

rooney mara, as erica albright, appears relatively briefly, but her presence is crucial. she is the catalyst for the entire story, and mara gives the role a calm intelligence that makes the breakup scene unforgettable. that opening exchange sets the tone for the whole film: mark’s inability to connect, his need to dominate, and his habit of turning rejection into aggression. it is one of the best opening sequences in modern cinema because it immediately establishes both character and theme.

david fincher’s direction is precise and controlled, which is exactly right for this material. he gives the film a cold, polished surface that mirrors the world it depicts. the visual style is sleek but never sterile; instead, it creates a sense of emotional distance that suits the story’s themes. fincher understands that this is a film about people who are constantly measuring themselves against others, and he stages scenes so that power shifts are always visible, even in small gestures or pauses.

trent reznor and atticus ross’s score is another major reason the film works so well. the music is eerie, propulsive, and modern, giving the movie a restless energy that matches the pace of the dialogue and the ambition of the characters. it helps turn what could have been a straightforward business drama into something more haunting and atmospheric. the score does not tell you how to feel; it deepens the unease already present in the story.

what makes the social network especially effective is that it understands the emotional cost of success. the film is full of people who are technically winning, but almost none of them seem happy. mark gets power, but loses trust. eduardo gets sidelined. the winklevoss twins get money, but not the recognition they wanted. even sean parker, played with slick charm by justin timberlake, feels like a figure who thrives on momentum rather than genuine connection. the movie suggests that in a world built on competition and image, victory can be another form of isolation.

the film also works because it is not nostalgic or sentimental about the rise of social media. it does not treat facebook as destiny or as a miracle of innovation. instead, it presents the platform as something born from a mix of talent, opportunism, insecurity, and social calculation. that makes the story feel more honest and more unsettling. the movie is less interested in whether mark changed the world than in what kind of person would be willing to do what he did to get there.

if there is a weakness, it is that the film’s emotional perspective is so tightly controlled that some viewers may find it chilly. the characters are often observed more than embraced, and the movie rarely pauses for warmth. but that coldness is also part of its power. it is a film about people who are brilliant at building systems and terrible at sustaining relationships, and the style reflects that truth.

overall, the social network is a superb film: intelligent, tense, beautifully acted, and emotionally devastating in a quiet way. it is one of those rare movies that feels both of its moment and timeless. beneath its story about coding, lawsuits, and billion-dollar companies, it is really about the pain of being left behind, the hunger to matter, and the way success can expose the worst parts of a person. it is a modern classic.

Imagine Earth like a spinning top that is leaning a little bit. That lean is called a tilt. As Earth travels around the Sun during the year, different parts of Earth get more sunlight or less sunlight.

- When your part of Earth is tilted toward the Sun, it gets more direct sunlight and longer days. That makes it warmer, so it’s summer.
- When your part of Earth is tilted away from the Sun, it gets less direct sunlight and shorter days. That makes it colder, so it’s winter.
- Spring and fall happen in between, when the sunlight is changing.

Mia wanted to learn how to move on her shiny blue bicycle.

At first, the bike felt very tall. Mia sat on the seat, held the handlebars, and looked at her dad with wide eyes.

“I feel wobbly,” she said.

“That is okay,” Dad said. “Everyone starts with a little wobble.”

Mia put on her helmet. It was red with tiny stars. Then Dad held the back of the bike while Mia pushed her feet on the pedals. The bicycle rolled slowly across the driveway.

“Look ahead,” Dad said. “Keep your feet moving.”

Mia tried again. The bike leaned a little to the left, then a little to the right. She laughed, then stopped, then tried once more.

After many tries, Dad let go for just a moment.

Mia did not notice at first. She was looking at the big oak tree at the end of the path. Her feet kept turning the pedals. The wheels spun smoothly. The breeze brushed her cheeks.

“I’m doing it!” Mia shouted.

She smiled so big that her cheeks hurt.

Soon she learned how to start, how to balance, and how to stop with her feet on the ground. Every day she practiced a little more. The wobbles grew smaller and smaller.

By the end of the week, Mia zoomed down the sidewalk with her friends cheering beside her.

She felt proud, brave, and happy.

And every time she saw her blue bicycle, she remembered that learning takes practice, patience, and a lot of smiles.
